# Security

Baseline security applies whatever the chosen authentication mode.

Marker after the identifier: a tool name = tooled constraint (the build or the commit fails); `guidance` = rule of conduct checked in review.

## Base rules

### Rules

- **CORE-030** · `gitleaks` — Secrets and environment-specific values come from environment variables; `.env.example` is committed and `.env` is ignored.
  Why: Configuration that differs per environment must never be a code change.
- **CORE-031** · `gitleaks` — No credential, token or private key is ever committed; the gitleaks pre-commit hook blocks the commit.
  Why: A secret in history is compromised even after it is removed.
- **CORE-032** · guidance — Actuator exposes only the `health` and `info` endpoints.
  Why: The other endpoints leak configuration, environment and heap dumps.
- **CORE-033** · guidance — CORS origins are an explicit list read from configuration; `*` is never used in `prod`.
  Why: A wildcard origin turns every browser into a client of the API.
- **CORE-034** · guidance — Default security headers (content type options, frame options, HSTS, cache control) are never disabled without an ADR.
  Why: Each header closes a class of browser attacks for free.
- **CORE-035** · `dependency-check` — Dependencies are scanned for known vulnerabilities in CI, and a critical finding blocks the release.
  Why: Most breaches exploit a known, already patched vulnerability.

### Anti-patterns

- **CORE-AP-030** · `gitleaks` — A password or API key written in `application.yaml`.
  Why: The value is committed, shared and impossible to rotate per environment.
  Instead: `${DB_PASSWORD}` in the configuration and the variable documented in `.env.example`.
- **CORE-AP-031** · guidance — `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: '*'` to "see everything".
  Why: Environment variables, beans and thread dumps become public.
  Instead: Keep `health,info` and read the rest from the logs or a metrics backend.
- **CORE-AP-032** · guidance — `allowedOrigins("*")` to make a local front end work.
  Why: The shortcut ships to production because nobody remembers it.
  Instead: The local origin in the `dev` configuration and the real one in `prod`.

### Expected environment variables

| Variable | Example | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `APP_ADMIN_USERNAME` | `admin` | Username of the bootstrap administrator (in-memory user store). |
| `APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | `change-me` | Password of the bootstrap administrator; never the example value in production. |

## Option `security-session`

HTTP session authentication with Spring Security (form login and HTTP basic), users from environment variables.

### Rules

- **SECS-001** · guidance — Every request outside `/actuator/health` and `/actuator/info` requires an authenticated session; the rule lives in `SecurityConfig` only.
  Why: One place to read to know what is public.
- **SECS-002** · `gitleaks` — Credentials come from `APP_ADMIN_USERNAME` and `APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD`; the in-memory user store is replaced by a real one before any multi-user use.
  Why: The skeleton must start with real authentication and no secret in the repository.
- **SECS-003** · guidance — CSRF protection stays enabled; single-page clients read the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie and send it back in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header.
  Why: A session cookie without CSRF protection lets any site act as the user.
- **SECS-004** · guidance — Tests run with `app.security.enabled=false` and Spring Security auto-configuration excluded; authorization itself is verified by `SecurityConfigTest`, which re-enables it explicitly.
  Why: Business tests must not need credentials; security rules get their own test.
- **SECS-005** · guidance — Passwords are stored and compared through the delegating `PasswordEncoder`; no `{noop}` password outside a test.
  Why: A clear-text password in memory or in a store is a breach waiting for a dump.

### Anti-patterns

- **SECS-AP-001** · guidance — `permitAll()` on `/api/**` "temporarily" to make a client work.
  Why: The temporary rule ships to production because nothing fails without it.
  Instead: Authenticate the client; use `SecurityConfigTest` to check the rule you actually want.
- **SECS-AP-002** · guidance — Disabling CSRF because a `POST` returns 403.
  Why: The 403 is the protection working; removing it opens every write endpoint.
  Instead: Send the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header from the client.
